lessons.title: Beyond CBS1: other Commission-approved contracts and addenda
lessons.body:
## Matching the form to the deal

The lesson on Commission-approved forms covered the basic rule: if a [[Commission-approved form]] exists and fits the transaction, you must use it. This lesson covers the forms beyond the standard residential contract (CBS1) that the exam likes to ask about, and when each one fits.

All current sales contracts on the Division of Real Estate's forms page are dated for use on and after **January 1, 2026**.

| Situation | Commission form |
|---|---|
| Rental house, duplex, fourplex or apartment building bought as an investment | **Income-Residential** contract (CBS2) |
| Office, retail, industrial or mixed-use property | **Commercial** contract (CBS3) |
| Vacant or agricultural land | **Land** contract (CBS4) |
| Homeowner in foreclosure who lives there, selling to a buyer who won't live there | **Residential (Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act)** contract (CBSF1) |
| Manufactured home sitting on a rented space in a park | **Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only)** (MHC1) |
| Land or commercial property that includes a manufactured home | Land or Commercial contract plus the **Manufactured Home Addendum** |

There is **no farm and ranch contract** on the current list. A ranch sale goes on the Land contract, with a Residential Addendum if there are houses, or to an attorney if it doesn't fit.

### Income-Residential, Commercial and Land

- **Income-Residential (CBS2):** built around tenants. It covers the rent roll, the existing leases, tenant estoppel statements and the transfer of security deposits.
- **Commercial (CBS3):** built for commercial due diligence, with deadlines for environmental (Phase I/II) review and an ADA evaluation. The Income-Residential contract has similar due-diligence items.
- **Land (CBS4):** focuses on water, minerals and growing crops.

When a commercial or land property has dwellings on it, the **[[Residential Addendum]]** brings in the residential disclosures, such as lead-based paint and carbon monoxide alarms.

### The Foreclosure Protection Act contract (CBSF1)

[[CBSF1]] is the Commission's version of the residential contract for sales to an [[equity purchaser]]. It applies when all of these are true:

- the home is residential,
- the seller lives there as a principal residence,
- the buyer will not live there, and
- the home is in foreclosure, or the buyer has notice that a loan on it is at least 30 days delinquent or in default.

The form works only if the deal is "clean":

- no assumption of the seller's obligations,
- no lease between buyer and seller (no leaseback),
- no option for the seller to buy the home back, and
- nothing of value paid to the seller until the cancellation right has expired.

The Notice of Cancellation and Seller Warning must be attached. Changing those conditions voids the contract. A deal with a leaseback or a buy-back option needs an attorney. If the deal is a short sale and a Short Sale Addendum is part of the contract, the Act does not apply.

### Manufactured homes (MHC1 and the addendum)

The **Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only)** is for a home on a rented park space. No land changes hands. Key differences from CBS1:

- **Title** passes by the home's **[[certificate of title]]**, not by a deed. The buyer may run a UCC search for liens. After closing, the buyer applies to the Department of Revenue for a new title.
- **The [[lot lease]]:** the seller delivers a copy, and the deal depends on the park owner approving the buyer and the home in writing and either assigning the lease or signing a new one. The buyer may terminate if the lease or the approval terms are unsatisfactory.
- The seller requests a status letter from the lot owner at least 14 days before closing.

The manufactured home line has its own Counterproposal, Amend/Extend, Agreement to Revive and Extension or Termination forms.

If the manufactured home sits on land being sold under the Land or Commercial contract, attach the **Manufactured Home Addendum**. It adds the home's serial number and VIN, the certificate-of-title steps and a UCC search.

> **Exam tip:** "Manufactured home in a park, on a rented space" points to the Lot Lease Only contract. If the seller owns the dirt under the home and it's being sold too, you're back to a real estate contract with an addendum.

## Leasing forms

There are **no Commission-approved leases or property management agreements**. What the Commission does provide:

- **[[Exclusive Right-to-Lease Listing Contract]]** (landlord side). The firm markets the property, shows it, screens applicants and negotiates a lease. As with the sale listing, the landlord picks landlord agency or transaction-brokerage, and **transaction-brokerage is the default** if neither box is checked. Compensation is earned if a lease is signed during the listing period by anyone, or if the broker produces a ready, willing and able tenant.
- **Exclusive Tenant Listing Contract** (tenant side). The broker finds a rental and negotiates for the tenant.
- **[[Brokerage Duties Addendum]] to Property Management Agreement.** Ongoing management (collecting rent, maintenance, deposits) makes the broker a general agent. The management agreement itself must be attorney-drafted. The Commission addendum attaches to it and sets out the brokerage relationship and duties.
- **[[Assignment of Lease]].** When a landlord sells a rented property, this form transfers the landlord's interest in the lease, and the security deposit, to the buyer at closing. The buyer takes on the landlord's obligations, and the tenant gets notice.

**The lease itself** must be drafted by the firm's own attorney or supplied by the owner. Borrowing another firm's attorney-drafted lease does not comply. If the owner supplies it, keep written confirmation of that.

## Addenda you should recognize

### Licensee Buy-Out Addendum

The [[Licensee Buy-Out Addendum]] is used when a **licensee is the buyer** of a seller's property, typically a broker or firm buying a client's home so the client can move on (for example, to buy the next home). Key features:

- It binds only the licensee who signs, unless the supervising broker of the brokerage working with the seller also signs.
- The **seller may terminate at any time** by written notice. The listing contract stays in effect, so the property can still sell to someone else.
- If the seller terminates, the seller reimburses the licensee's out-of-pocket expenses up to a stated cap.
- It strips out parts of the contract that don't fit a buy-out, including the appraisal clause, liquidated damages and the seller-default remedies.
- The licensee keeps any profit or loss on resale.

The broker is acting as a principal here, so the usual rules apply: disclose your licensed status in writing and use the Commission form.

### Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement

The [[Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement]] is a seller rent-back. The seller hands over the deed but stays in the home for a short time.

- It is for **short-term residential occupancy of no more than 60 days**. A longer stay calls for a real residential lease.
- Rent is paid to the buyer in advance at closing. A security deposit (no more than two months' rent) is held by the buyer and returned within 30 days after the term ends, as Colorado law requires.
- The buyer insures the property as owner. The buyer can enter on 24 hours' notice, or immediately in an emergency.
- The seller may end the occupancy early on 5 days' written notice.
- A seller who doesn't leave on time faces eviction and damages.

**Pre-closing occupancy** (the buyer moving in before closing) has **no Commission form**. It's riskier, because the buyer has possession but no title. That agreement needs an attorney.

> **Exam tip:** Seller stays **after** closing = Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement (60 days max). Buyer moves in **before** closing = no Commission form, so get an attorney.

### Source of Water Addendum

The [[Source of Water Addendum]] records where the home's water comes from. The seller checks one option: a **well** (with the permit number, and whether a copy of the permit is attached), a **water provider** (with contact information), or **some other source** described in writing. It warns the buyer that some providers rely on nonrenewable groundwater and suggests checking long-term supply.

### Short Sale Addendum

There are two versions: one for the **listing contract** and one for the **purchase contract**. Use them when liens exceed the price and lienholders must agree to take less. The sale terminates if lender approval doesn't arrive by the Short Sale Acceptance Deadline. Details are in the earlier addenda lesson.

### Exchange Addendum

The [[Exchange Addendum]] supports a [[Section 1031 exchange]]. Either the buyer or the seller can be the exchanging party.

- The other party agrees to cooperate **at no additional cost or liability** to itself.
- The exchanging party may assign its contract rights to set up the exchange.
- **The exchange is not a condition of the deal.** The contract binds both parties whether or not the exchange works out.

### Other addenda and closing forms

The Open Listing and Exclusive Brokerage Listing Addenda modify the Exclusive Right-to-Sell Listing Contract. The Earnest Money Receipt, Closing Instructions, Closing Statement and Earnest Money Release were covered with the residential contract.

## When a non-Commission form is allowed

If no Commission form fits, a broker may use a form drafted by the firm's Colorado attorney, a form a party supplies, a lender or government form, or a Colorado Bar Association form, within the limits covered in the practice-of-law lesson. A broker who is a party may have counsel prepare a form, but it must say conspicuously that it is **not** Commission-approved. The broker never drafts the legal language.

> **Exam tip:** Forms are revised often, and the Division posts each version with a mandatory-use date. Versions for use on and after January 1, 2027 are already posted for information (for example, the Exchange Addendum is renamed the "Section 1031 Exchange Addendum," and the Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement has substantive changes). Always confirm you're on the current version.

lessons.title: Homeowners' associations and the Colorado Common Interest Ownership Act
lessons.body:
## What a common interest community is

A [[common interest community]] (CIC) is real estate where owning your unit or lot obligates you to pay for common property or for other units' expenses. Condominiums, most townhome communities and planned subdivisions with an HOA are typical examples. In Colorado these communities are governed by the **[[Colorado Common Interest Ownership Act]]** (CCIOA), C.R.S. 38-33.3.

Some quick points:

- CCIOA applies to communities **created on or after July 1, 1992** (C.R.S. 38-33.3-115), with limited exceptions for some small or limited-expense communities.
- For communities created **before** July 1, 1992, the Act generally does not apply, except for a list of sections in C.R.S. 38-33.3-117 that reach them for events after July 1, 1992 (later amendments added more). The lien section is on that list. Older condominiums otherwise remain partly under prior law, such as the Condominium Ownership Act.
- CCIOA's protections **can't be waived** or varied by agreement except where the Act allows.
- The Act limits what HOAs can prohibit. Examples include flags, political signs, drought-tolerant landscaping and EV chargers.

## The governing documents

| Document | What it is | Who creates or changes it |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Declaration]]** | The **recorded** document that creates the community. It defines units and common elements, allocates assessments and sets use restrictions (the CC&Rs) | The developer records it. Owners amend it by vote |
| **[[Bylaws]]** | How the association runs: board size, elections, meetings, officers | The association |
| **[[Rules and regulations]]** | Day-to-day rules: parking, pets, trash, pools | The board, within the declaration's authority |
| Articles of incorporation | Form the association as a legal entity (usually a nonprofit corporation) | Filed with the Secretary of State |

The **declaration is the top document**. Bylaws and rules can't contradict it. Associations must also adopt written governance policies, including a collection policy and a covenant-enforcement policy. An HOA can't fine an owner without a written fine policy that gives notice and a chance to be heard.

## Assessments and the HOA lien

**[[Assessments]]** are the owners' shares of the community's common expenses, allocated by a formula in the declaration. There are two main kinds:

- **Regular assessments:** the monthly or quarterly dues that fund the budget, including reserves.
- **[[Special assessment]]s:** one-time charges for a specific need, such as a new roof or a lawsuit.

Generally there is no statutory cap on dues increases unless the governing documents create one.

### The statutory lien

Under C.R.S. 38-33.3-316, the association has a statutory lien on the unit for assessments and fines. Late charges, attorney fees and interest can also be secured by the lien. Recording the declaration perfects it, so no separate lien filing is needed. The lien is extinguished unless the association starts enforcement within **six years** after the full amount of assessments becomes due.

### Priority: the "super-lien"

The HOA lien is ahead of all other liens on the unit **except**:
1. liens recorded **before the declaration**,
2. the **first mortgage or deed of trust** recorded before the assessment became delinquent, and
3. **real estate taxes** and other governmental assessments.

The twist is the **[[super-lien]]**. Even against that first mortgage, the HOA's lien has priority for up to **six months of regular common-expense assessments**: the amount, based on the association's budget and without acceleration, that would have come due in the six months before the association or a senior lienholder starts an action or foreclosure. Fines, late fees and legal fees don't get that super-priority.

To **foreclose** its lien, the balance secured by the lien must equal or exceed six months of common-expense assessments, and the board must pass a **recorded vote** authorizing legal action against that specific unit. Fines, fees, late charges and interest can be secured by the lien but can't by themselves be the basis of a CCIOA foreclosure.

> **Exam tip:** "How much of an HOA's lien beats a first mortgage in Colorado?" Answer: up to six months of regular assessments. Property taxes still come first.

### Registration

Associations must **register annually** with the Division of Real Estate's HOA Information and Resource Center. An association that isn't validly registered **can't enforce its assessment lien** until it registers again. Its existing liens aren't wiped out, and its rights come back once it is registered.

## Disclosure that the property is in a CIC

**C.R.S. 38-35.7-102** requires every contract to buy and sell residential property in a common interest community to include a disclosure in **bold-faced, clearly legible type**, substantially in the statute's wording. In substance it tells the buyer:

- the property is in a CIC and the owner must be a member of the association and follow its declaration, bylaws and rules,
- the governing documents impose financial obligations, including assessments,
- unpaid assessments can become a lien and can lead to the property being sold,
- changes to the property may need architectural approval, and
- the buyer should look into the association's finances and read the governing documents.

The **seller** is responsible for it. A seller who fails to give it can be sued by the buyer for actual damages it caused, plus court costs. The seller has a defense if the buyer already knew. The Commission residential contract carries this [[Common Interest Community Disclosure]] in Section 7, so using the current form satisfies it.

## Association documents under the Commission contract

The residential contract (Section 7) puts the burden on the **seller**:

- **What:** the [[association documents]].
  - Governing documents (declaration, articles, bylaws, rules, party-wall agreements, governance policies).
  - Minutes.
  - The association's insurance list.
  - The list of regular and special assessments.
  - Financials: budget, financial statements, reserves, audit or review, fees due at closing, and any **reserve study**.
  - Any notice of a **construction defect action** from the past six months.
- **When and who pays:** by the **Association Documents Deadline**, at the seller's expense. The seller may have the association send them. The Seller Association Authorization form lets the seller authorize someone to request them.
- **Buyer's escape hatch:** by the **Association Documents Termination Deadline**, the buyer may terminate if anything in them is unsatisfactory, in the buyer's sole subjective discretion. If the documents arrive late, the buyer has **10 days after receipt** (and no later than closing). If the buyer doesn't terminate in time, the buyer accepts the documents.

Money items:
- The seller requests the **status letter** and pays its fee.
- Regular assessments are **prorated** to closing.
- Reserves aren't credited back to the seller unless the governing documents say so.
- A checkbox decides who pays **special assessments levied before closing**. The seller pays special assessments for improvements already installed as of the buyer's signing date.

## HOA managers: no state license

Colorado **licensed community association managers from 2015 to 2019**. The program **expired June 30, 2019**, after the governor vetoed the bill to continue it. Today the state does **not** license HOA managers.

The **[[HOA Information and Resource Center]]** (in the Division of Real Estate) registers associations, educates owners, logs complaints and reports to the legislature. It is **not a regulator**. It doesn't investigate, mediate, fine or enforce. HOA disputes are civil matters handled through the governing documents, mediation or court.

> **Exam tip:** If an answer choice says the Division or the Real Estate Commission will discipline an HOA or its manager, it's wrong. There's no license to discipline, and the HOA Center has no enforcement power.

## What brokers should check

- **Is it in a CIC?** Look for a declaration in the title work, dues on the MLS and metro district information. Many homes are in both an HOA and a metro district.
- **Read the restrictions** that matter to this buyer: rentals, pets, parking, RVs, home businesses, architectural control.
- **Finances:** budget, reserves, reserve study, pending or likely special assessments, delinquency levels.
- **Litigation:** construction defect notices and other lawsuits.
- **Closing costs:** status letter, transfer and record-change fees, working capital contributions.
- **Calendar the Association Documents deadlines.** Don't interpret the documents for the buyer. Encourage the buyer to read them and get legal advice on anything complicated.

questions.stem: A seller owns a manufactured home that sits on a rented space in a mobile home park. Which Commission-approved contract fits the sale of the home?
choices: Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Land) with the Manufactured Home Addendum
Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Income-Residential)
questions.explanation: When the home sits on a leased lot, no land changes hands, so the Commission's Lot Lease Only manufactured home contract is the form. The Manufactured Home Addendum is for a home that comes with land sold under the Land or Commercial contract.

questions.stem: How does title to the home pass under the Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only)?
choices: By the home's certificate of title; the buyer then applies to the Department of Revenue
By a special warranty deed from the seller, recorded with the county clerk and recorder
By assignment of the lot lease, which carries ownership of the home along with it
By a quitclaim deed from the park owner, recorded in the county where the park is located
questions.explanation: A manufactured home on a leased lot is titled like a vehicle. The seller delivers the certificate of title, and after closing the buyer applies to the Department of Revenue for a new title. No deed is used because no land is conveyed.

questions.stem: A homeowner who lives in her house is two months behind on her mortgage and in foreclosure. An investor who won't live there wants to buy it and lease it back to her. What should the brokers do about the contract?
choices: Use the Foreclosure Protection Act contract and add the leaseback terms in Additional Provisions
Use the standard Residential contract, since the seller is cooperating and the Act is optional
Use the Licensee Buy-Out Addendum, which lets the seller terminate and stay on as a tenant
Have an attorney prepare it, since a leaseback can't be used with the Commission's CBSF1
questions.explanation: The Commission's CBSF1 requires that there be no lease between buyer and seller, no repurchase option and no assumption of the seller's obligations. Changing those conditions voids the form, so a leaseback deal needs an attorney-drafted contract.

questions.stem: The seller needs to stay in the house for three weeks after closing while her new home is finished. Which Commission-approved form fits?
choices: Residential lease drafted by the listing broker
Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement
Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract
Assignment of Lease
questions.explanation: The Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement is the Commission's seller rent-back form for short-term residential occupancy after closing. Brokers can't draft a lease themselves, and Amend/Extend changes the contract's terms rather than creating an occupancy arrangement.

questions.stem: A seller wants to remain in the home for four months after closing. Why is the Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement a poor fit?
choices: It may be used only for commercial property, not for a residence
It requires the seller to pay rent monthly in arrears to the buyer
It is limited to short-term stays of no more than 60 days
It may be used only when the buyer is a real estate licensee
questions.explanation: The form states it is only for short-term residential occupancy not exceeding 60 days. A longer stay needs a residential lease, and since there is no Commission-approved lease, that lease comes from an attorney.

questions.stem: Buyers want to move into the home a week before closing. Which Commission-approved form covers pre-closing occupancy?
choices: None exists, so an attorney should prepare the occupancy agreement
The Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement, with the buyer and seller roles reversed
The Exclusive Tenant Listing Contract, signed by the buyer as the tenant
The Earnest Money Receipt, noting the early possession date on it
questions.explanation: The Commission's forms list includes only a post-closing (seller rent-back) occupancy form. Letting a buyer take possession before closing has its own risks and needs an attorney-drafted agreement. Reworking the post-closing form would be drafting.

questions.stem: A broker's firm offers to buy a listing client's home so the client can buy her next home without a sale contingency. Which Commission form modifies the purchase contract for this?
choices: Exchange Addendum
Licensee Buy-Out Addendum
Short Sale Addendum (Contract to Buy & Sell)
Residential Addendum
questions.explanation: The Licensee Buy-Out Addendum is used when a licensee is the buyer of the seller's property. It removes provisions that don't fit a buy-out and lets the seller terminate at any time while the listing continues.

questions.stem: Under the Licensee Buy-Out Addendum, the seller finds a better offer and terminates the buy-out contract. What is the seller's obligation to the licensee buyer?
choices: Pay the licensee the full resale profit the licensee expected to make
Pay liquidated damages equal to the earnest money the licensee deposited
Nothing, because terminating the buy-out also ends the listing contract
Reimburse the licensee's out-of-pocket expenses, up to the stated cap
questions.explanation: The seller may terminate at any time by written notice. The seller then reimburses the licensee's out-of-pocket expenses up to the stated cap. The listing contract stays in effect, and liquidated damages are deleted by the addendum.

questions.stem: A seller wants a Section 1031 exchange and the parties sign the Commission's Exchange Addendum. The seller can't find replacement property. What is the effect on the sale?
choices: The contract stays binding; the exchange is not a condition of it
The contract terminates automatically and the earnest money is returned
Closing is extended until the seller identifies a replacement property
The buyer must cover any added tax the seller owes because the exchange failed
questions.explanation: The Exchange Addendum says the parties remain bound whether or not the exchange happens. It doesn't change any contract dates. The cooperating party helps only at no added cost or liability to itself.

questions.stem: A landlord wants a brokerage to market his rental house and find a tenant. Which Commission-approved form sets up that relationship?
choices: Exclusive Tenant Listing Contract
Exclusive Brokerage Listing Addendum to the ERTS
Exclusive Right-to-Lease Listing Contract
Brokerage Disclosure to Buyer
questions.explanation: The Exclusive Right-to-Lease Listing Contract is the landlord-side leasing listing. The Exclusive Tenant Listing Contract is for a broker representing or helping a tenant who is looking for a rental.

questions.stem: A brokerage firm starting a leasing practice needs a residential lease form. What does the Commission require?
choices: Use the Commission-approved residential lease
Copy another firm's attorney-drafted lease
Have the firm's managing broker write a lease based on the Exclusive Right-to-Lease contract
Have the firm's own attorney draft the lease, or use a lease the owner supplies
questions.explanation: There are no Commission-approved leases. The Commission position is that each firm's own attorney drafts its lease, and borrowing another firm's attorney form doesn't comply. If the owner provides the lease, the broker keeps written confirmation of that.

questions.stem: A broker will collect rent, handle maintenance and hold deposits for a landlord on an ongoing basis. What paperwork fits?
choices: An attorney-drafted management agreement plus the Brokerage Duties Addendum
The Exclusive Right-to-Lease Listing Contract, renewed each year
The Commission-approved Property Management Agreement and its addendum
The Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement, naming the broker as the landlord's manager
questions.explanation: Ongoing management makes the broker a general agent and needs a management agreement drafted by an attorney, since the Commission has none. The Commission's Brokerage Duties Addendum attaches to it to set out the brokerage relationship and duties.

questions.stem: A landlord is selling a fourplex with tenants in place. What is the Commission's Assignment of Lease used for at closing?
choices: Letting an existing tenant sublet the unit to a new tenant before closing
Moving the landlord's lease rights and deposits to the buyer at closing
Ending the existing leases so the buyer gets vacant possession at closing
Assigning the buyer's purchase contract to a new buyer before closing
questions.explanation: The Assignment of Lease moves the seller-landlord's lease rights and the security deposit to the buyer at closing. The buyer assumes the landlord's obligations, and the tenant is notified of the new owner.

questions.stem: The seller's home is served by a private well. What does the Source of Water Addendum ask the seller to provide?
choices: A water quality test from a state-certified laboratory
The name of the nearest municipal water provider, if any
The well permit number and whether a copy is attached
An engineer's estimate of the aquifer's remaining life
questions.explanation: For a well, the seller gives the well permit number and indicates whether a copy is attached. For a water provider, the seller gives the provider's contact information. Otherwise the seller describes the actual source.

questions.stem: Under CCIOA, which document is recorded and creates the common interest community?
choices: The declaration
The bylaws
The rules and regulations
The annual budget
questions.explanation: The declaration is the recorded instrument that creates the community and sets out units, common elements, assessment allocation and restrictions. Bylaws govern how the association operates. Rules are the board's day-to-day regulations.

questions.stem: A unit owner stops paying HOA dues and the first-mortgage lender forecloses. Under C.R.S. 38-33.3-316, how much of the association's lien has priority over that first deed of trust?
choices: None. A first deed of trust always comes ahead of HOA liens
Up to six months of regular common-expense assessments
All unpaid assessments, plus fines, late fees and attorney fees
Up to twelve months of assessments, plus interest and costs
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 38-33.3-316(2)(b) gives the HOA lien priority over a first deed of trust for up to six months of common-expense assessments based on the association's budget (the amount that would have come due in the six months before enforcement began). Fines and fees don't get that priority, and real estate taxes still come ahead of the HOA lien.

questions.stem: A seller of a condominium unit uses a contract that leaves out the common interest community disclosure required by C.R.S. 38-35.7-102. What is the consequence?
choices: The contract is automatically void and the earnest money returned
The listing broker's license is automatically suspended by the Division
The buyer may rescind the purchase at any time before the deed is recorded
The buyer may sue the seller for actual damages plus court costs
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 38-35.7-102 puts the disclosure duty on the seller. If it is missing, the buyer may recover actual damages directly and proximately caused by the failure, plus court costs; the seller has a defense if the buyer had actual or constructive knowledge. The contract isn't automatically void.

questions.stem: The seller delivers the association documents five days after the Association Documents Deadline. Under the Commission residential contract, how long does the buyer have to terminate based on them?
choices: The original Association Documents Termination Deadline still controls
3 days after receipt
10 days after receipt, but no later than closing
Until 30 days after closing
questions.explanation: When association documents arrive late, the buyer may terminate by notice received within 10 days after receiving them. If that date would fall after closing, the notice is due by closing. If no timely notice is given, the buyer accepts the documents.

questions.stem: An HOA's annual registration with the Division of Real Estate has lapsed. What is the effect on its assessment lien?
choices: It can't enforce the lien until it registers again; the lien survives
The lien is permanently extinguished and must be re-recorded
The Real Estate Commission fines the board members for the lapse
Nothing, because registration with the Division is voluntary
questions.explanation: Under CCIOA's registration section, an unregistered association can't enforce its assessment lien or use certain other remedies until it registers. Existing liens survive, and its rights come back once registration is current.

questions.stem: A homeowner wants to file a complaint against her HOA's management company for mishandling association funds. She asks a broker which state agency licenses HOA managers. What is accurate?
choices: The Real Estate Commission licenses HOA managers and can revoke a license
The HOA Information and Resource Center will investigate and fine the manager
HOA managers must hold a Colorado broker license, so the Commission can act
No state agency does; CAM licensing ended in 2019
questions.explanation: Colorado's community association manager licensing program ran from 2015 until it expired on June 30, 2019, so no state agency licenses HOA managers now. The HOA Information and Resource Center educates, registers associations and logs complaints, but it doesn't investigate, mediate or enforce. Disputes are civil matters.

cards.front: Commission contract for a rental fourplex bought as an investment?
cards.back: Income-Residential contract (CBS2).

cards.front: Commission contract for vacant acreage?
cards.back: Land contract (CBS4). Add the Residential Addendum if there are dwellings.

cards.front: Is there a current Commission farm and ranch contract?
cards.back: No. It isn't on the current forms list. Use the Land contract, or an attorney if it doesn't fit.

cards.front: CBSF1 is used when…
cards.back: The seller occupies the home as a principal residence, it's in foreclosure (or 30+ days delinquent), and the buyer won't live there. This is the Foreclosure Protection Act version of the residential contract.

cards.front: Three things that knock a deal out of the CBSF1 form
cards.back: A leaseback, a seller repurchase option, or the buyer assuming the seller's obligations. Any of these needs an attorney.

cards.front: Manufactured home on a rented park space: which form?
cards.back: Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only), MHC1.

cards.front: MHC1: what must the park (lot owner) do?
cards.back: Approve the buyer and the home in writing and assign the lot lease or sign a new one. The buyer may terminate if the terms are unsatisfactory.

cards.front: Manufactured Home Addendum attaches to…
cards.back: The Land or Commercial contract, when the property includes a manufactured home.

cards.front: Are there Commission-approved leases or property management agreements?
cards.back: No. The firm's own attorney drafts them, or the owner supplies the form.

cards.front: Exclusive Right-to-Lease vs. Exclusive Tenant Listing
cards.back: Right-to-Lease: landlord hires the firm to find a tenant. Exclusive Tenant: tenant hires the firm to find a rental.

cards.front: Brokerage Duties Addendum attaches to…
cards.back: An attorney-drafted property management agreement. It sets out the landlord agency or transaction-brokerage duties.

cards.front: Assignment of Lease (Commission form)
cards.back: A landlord selling a rented property assigns the lease and security deposit to the buyer at closing. The buyer assumes the landlord's obligations.

cards.front: Licensee Buy-Out Addendum: who is the buyer?
cards.back: A licensee, such as a broker or firm buying a client's property. The seller may terminate at any time and reimburses expenses up to a cap.

cards.front: Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement: maximum term
cards.back: No more than 60 days of short-term residential occupancy. A longer stay needs a residential lease.

cards.front: Buyer moving in before closing: which Commission form?
cards.back: None. Pre-closing occupancy needs an attorney-drafted agreement.

cards.front: Exchange Addendum: is the 1031 exchange a condition of closing?
cards.back: No. The contract binds both parties whether or not the exchange happens. The other party cooperates at no added cost or liability.

cards.front: Source of Water Addendum: the seller's three choices
cards.back: A well (permit number), a water provider (contact info), or another source described in writing.

cards.front: CCIOA citation and which communities it covers
cards.back: C.R.S. 38-33.3. Applies to communities created on or after July 1, 1992; only listed sections (38-33.3-117) reach older communities.

cards.front: HOA super-lien in Colorado
cards.back: Up to 6 months of regular common-expense assessments (budget-based, no acceleration) has priority over a first deed of trust. Taxes still come first.

cards.front: HOA lien: what comes ahead of it?
cards.back: Liens recorded before the declaration, a first mortgage recorded before delinquency (except the 6-month super-lien), and property taxes and governmental assessments.

cards.front: C.R.S. 38-35.7-102 disclosure: format and responsible party
cards.back: Bold-faced, clearly legible type in the contract. The seller is responsible, and the buyer may sue for actual damages if it's missing.

cards.front: Association documents arrive late: buyer's termination window
cards.back: 10 days after receipt, but no later than closing.

cards.front: Who pays the HOA status letter fee under the residential contract?
cards.back: The seller.

cards.front: Colorado HOA manager licensing today
cards.back: None. The CAM licensing program expired June 30, 2019.

cards.front: HOA Information and Resource Center: what it does and doesn't do
cards.back: Registers HOAs, educates owners and logs complaints. It doesn't investigate, mediate, fine or enforce.

cards.front: When can an HOA foreclose its assessment lien under CCIOA?
cards.back: When the balance equals or exceeds 6 months of common-expense assessments and the board has authorized action against that unit by recorded vote. Fines alone can't be foreclosed.

cards.front: Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement: security deposit
cards.back: No more than two months' rent, held by the buyer and returned within 30 days after the term.

glossary.definition: A contract, addendum, notice or disclosure promulgated by the Colorado Real Estate Commission. Brokers must use it whenever one exists and fits the transaction.
A Commission addendum attached to the Commercial or Land contract when the property includes dwellings. It brings in residential disclosures such as lead-based paint and carbon monoxide alarms.
The Commission's Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential) (Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act). It is for buying an owner-occupied home in foreclosure when the buyer won't live there.
Under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act, generally a person who acquires title to a residence in foreclosure other than to live in it as a personal residence. The Act lists further exceptions.
The state-issued title document for a manufactured home that hasn't been converted to real property. It transfers ownership instead of a deed.
A rental agreement for the space a manufactured home sits on, usually in a park. A buyer of the home must be approved by the lot owner and take over the lease or sign a new one.
The Commission's landlord-side listing contract. It hires a brokerage to market a property for lease and find a tenant.
aliases: Exclusive Right to Lease Listing Contract

glossary.definition: The Commission's Brokerage Duties Addendum to Property Management Agreement. It attaches to an attorney-drafted management agreement and sets out the brokerage relationship and duties.
aliases: Brokerage Duties Addendum to Property Management Agreement

glossary.definition: A Commission optional form a landlord-seller uses to transfer existing leases and security deposits to the buyer at closing. The buyer assumes the landlord's obligations.
A Commission addendum for a purchase contract in which a licensee buys the seller's property. The seller may terminate at any time and reimburses the licensee's expenses up to a stated cap.
A Commission optional form for a seller rent-back: the seller stays in the home after closing for a short term of no more than 60 days.
A Commission addendum in which the seller states whether water comes from a well (with permit number), a water provider, or another described source.

A Commission addendum that lets either party structure the sale as a Section 1031 exchange. The other party cooperates at no added cost, and the contract binds both parties even if the exchange fails.
A tax-deferred like-kind exchange of investment or business real estate under Internal Revenue Code Section 1031.
Real estate where owning a unit or lot obligates the owner to pay for common elements or other units' expenses. Examples are condos, townhome communities and HOA subdivisions.

C.R.S. 38-33.3, the statute governing Colorado common interest communities and their associations. It applies to communities created on or after July 1, 1992, and only listed sections apply to older ones.
The recorded document that creates a common interest community. It defines units and common elements, allocates assessments and sets restrictions.
The association's rules for running itself: board, elections, officers and meetings.
Day-to-day rules adopted by an association's board, such as parking, pets and amenities. They must be consistent with the declaration.
Owners' shares of a common interest community's common expenses, allocated by the declaration and secured by a statutory lien.
A one-time association charge for a specific expense, such as a major repair, on top of regular dues.
Colorado's limited priority for an HOA's assessment lien over a first deed of trust, for up to six months of regular common-expense assessments.

The bold-type statement C.R.S. 38-35.7-102 requires in contracts for residential property in a CIC. It covers membership, assessments, liens, architectural approval and the buyer's need to investigate.
Under the Commission contract: the governing documents, minutes, insurance list, assessment list, financials and reserve study, and recent construction-defect notices the seller must provide.
A statement from the association showing a unit's assessments and amounts owed, used at closing. Under the residential contract the seller requests it and pays the fee.
The Division of Real Estate office that registers HOAs, educates owners and logs complaints. It is not a regulator and has no enforcement power.
